result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_arborescence()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Find a maximum-weight spanning arborescence of a directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm). twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_arborescence()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Find a maximum-weight spanning arborescence of a directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm). title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_arborescence()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Find a maximum-weight spanning arborescence of a directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm). page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a maximum-weight spanning arborescence of a directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L69549-L69647){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.maximum_spanning_arborescence( weight_attr=None, include=None, exclude=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximum spanning arborescence](../assets/graphs/maximum-spanning-arborescence.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A weighted directed graph: A→B (3), B→C (−2), A→C (−5), and C→D (4). Node C can only be reached through a negative edge, and a spanning arborescence must reach every node, so it takes the less costly B→C: the tree A→B, B→C, C→D in the accent color, total 3 − 2 + 4 = 5, with A→C faded. The card contrasts it with the maximum branching, which leaves C without a parent and keeps only A→B and C→D, total 7." width="100%"} A spanning arborescence is a directed tree that reaches every node from a single root: the root has no incoming edge and every other node has exactly one. Among all spanning arborescences (over every possible root), this method returns one with the largest total edge weight. Unlike `maximum_branching()`, it must use exactly `n - 1` edges, so it may include low or negative weights when that is the only way to reach a node. Typical uses include choosing the most plausible single-origin explanation of a process (a broadcast or contagion tree, a phylogeny with a common ancestor) and dependency parsing, where every word but the root takes exactly one head. `include=` and `exclude=` restrict the search to the arborescences that use every included edge and none of the excluded ones. Self-loops are never chosen, and the original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding the weights. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (`1.0` on an unweighted graph), as it is for `"weight"`. Under any other name, every edge must hold a number. [include]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges the result must contain, as edge IDs or `(u, v)` node pairs (a pair stands for every edge from `u` to `v`). [exclude]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges the result must not contain, given the same way. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new directed graph with every node of the original (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and the `n - 1` arborescence edges (weights and attributes copied). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected, an edge value is NaN, `weight_attr=` names an attribute that an edge lacks or holds as a non-number, no spanning arborescence exists (no single node can reach all the others), or none uses every included edge and avoids every excluded one. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Edmonds' algorithm is run with weights ordered lexicographically as (edge count, total weight): every edge counts as one unit of the first component, so the optimum first takes as many edges as possible and only then maximizes the weight. This makes the result a spanning arborescence whenever one exists, without adding a large constant to the weights (which would cost floating-point precision). Included edges get one more component ranked before both, so the optimum takes all of them whenever it can, and excluded edges are dropped up front. It runs in $O(V E)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} C can only be reached through negative-weight edges, so `maximum_branching()` leaves it without a parent. The spanning arborescence has to reach it, and takes the less costly of its two in-edges, B -> C (-2): ::: {#542d6cc9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", 3.0), ("B", "C", -2.0), ("A", "C", -5.0), ("C", "D", 4.0)]) tree = g.maximum_spanning_arborescence() tree.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A->B', 'B->C', 'C->D'] ``` ::: ::: The arborescence has `n - 1 = 3` edges and total weight 5, while the maximum branching has only two edges (total 7) and splits into two trees: ::: {#3f8598f5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree.count_edges(), g.maximum_branching().get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (3, ['A->B', 'C->D']) ``` ::: ::: If no node can reach all the others, there is no spanning arborescence: ::: {#f243b247 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} split = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) split.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "B")]) try: split.maximum_spanning_arborescence() except ValueError as err: print(err) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` no spanning arborescence exists: not every node can be reached from a single root ``` ::: :::
